title: What Paint Is Made Of
description: Pigment, dye and binder, from a 100,000-year-old ochre kit to tempera, fresco and oil

concepts.title: You Cannot Discover a Colour
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask a chemist who has just made a new blue how it feels to discover a colour, and you may be corrected. "Color is a part of a spectrum, so you can't discover a color," says Mas Subramanian of Oregon State University, whose laboratory produced a brand-new blue pigment in 2009. "You can only discover a material that is a particular color." That idea runs through this whole topic. A pigment is a material that absorbs certain parts of the spectrum and reflects the rest, and the light it sends back is the colour you see. If you have taken Inorganic Chemistry, you have met one way this works: electrons in metal ions jumping between energy levels as they absorb visible light. Pigments use that trick and several others.

To make paint you need two ingredients. As the National Gallery in London explains, paint is made by mixing a pigment, which supplies the colour, with a medium, which binds the particles of pigment together.1 The medium, or binder, might be egg, oil, gum or lime. Pigments themselves can be minerals dug from the ground, compounds made in a furnace or a flask, or even dyes from plants and animals.

So what separates a pigment from a dye? Conservators at the University of Delaware put it this way: dyes are soluble and usually absorbed by the material, while pigments are insoluble and lie on top of it.2 A dye soaks into a wool thread; a pigment is a powder of coloured grains that must be glued in place. The two can meet. Fix a dissolved dye onto a colourless mineral powder and you get a lake pigment. Van Gogh's bright pink eosin was sold as "geranium lake", and analysis of one of his paintings found it, most likely, precipitated onto an aluminium-based substrate.

The difference matters for everything that follows. Grains of mineral can survive for tens of thousands of years, while many colours made from living things are far more fragile, as the last lesson shows. Along the way you will meet colours cooked in furnaces, scraped from snails and dug from tombs.

concepts.title: The First Paint Kit: Ochre at Blombos Cave
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest colours were dug from the ground. Ochre is the archaeologists' word for an earth or rock containing red or yellow oxides or hydroxides of iron. Yellow ochre owes its colour to the mineral goethite, red ochre to haematite, and fire turns one into the other: heating drives water out of goethite and leaves red haematite, as in the reaction below.

On the southern Cape coast of South Africa, about 300 km east of Cape Town, lies Blombos Cave. In 2008 a team led by Christopher Henshilwood uncovered a workshop there where people had made an ochre-rich paint about 100,000 years ago and stored it in two abalone shells.1 The two toolkits included ochre, bone, charcoal, grindstones and hammerstones. The team reconstructed the recipe: pieces of ochre were rubbed on quartzite slabs to make a fine red powder, then combined with heated crushed mammal bone, charcoal, stone chips and a liquid, poured into the shells and gently stirred, probably with a bone. The surrounding sand was dated by optically stimulated luminescence.

Nobody knows exactly what the mixture was for; decoration, painting and skin protection have all been suggested. What the kit does show, Henshilwood argues, is planning: people 100,000 years ago could source, combine and store substances, which implies an elementary knowledge of chemistry. If you met the engraved ochre from the same cave in the Before Writing topic, this is a different kind of evidence: not a single symbol but a recipe.

The chemistry of ochre explains a surprise at Pompeii. Most of the wall paintings from Pompeii are decorated with red and yellow colours, but the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD changed some of them.2 The heat of the eruption turned some yellow-painted areas red by converting goethite into haematite. In a 2019 study, Iker Marcaida and colleagues baked nine yellow fragments from Pompeii at temperatures from 200 to 400 °C to estimate how hot the volcanic flow was when it struck the walls. Some "Pompeian red" was yellow when the Romans painted it.

concepts.title: Egg, Lime and Oil: Gluing Colour Down
concepts.contentHtml:
A pigment is only as good as its binder. For most of European painting's history, three binders mattered most:

  • Egg tempera uses egg yolk as the medium. According to the National Gallery it has been used since Antiquity, most early Italian paintings are in it, and it became less common after 1500.1
  • Fresco, from the Italian for "fresh", is painted on lime plaster. In buon fresco the paint goes onto the final smooth layer, the intonaco, while it is still wet, so only as much plaster as can be painted in one day is spread on the wall. Each day's patch is a giornata, and the method bonds the paint to the wall.
  • Oil paint binds pigment in a drying oil such as linseed or walnut, which slowly hardens in air. Lead white even acts as a catalyst for this drying.

You can see two binders side by side in the National Gallery in London. Michelangelo's two unfinished panels there differ: the Manchester Madonna is in egg tempera, while The Entombment, begun around 1500, is in oil on wood. Michelangelo still painted the oil picture one figure at a time, as if it were tempera, the way he had learned in Ghirlandaio's workshop.

Who invented oil painting? The usual answer, popularised by Giorgio Vasari, is Jan van Eyck in 15th-century Flanders. It is a myth. Oil painting was documented by the 12th century, and in 2008 scientists at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble found drying oils in Buddhist murals from the caves of Bamiyan in Afghanistan, behind the giant Buddha statues the Taliban destroyed in 2001.2 The murals, painted in the mid-7th century, show Buddhas in vermilion robes sitting cross-legged amid palm leaves and mythical creatures. Twelve of the 50 caves were painted in oil, perhaps walnut and poppy-seed oil, which the team called the earliest clear example of oil painting in the world.3

title: Egyptian Blue: The First Synthetic Colour
description: A blue cooked from sand and copper 5,000 years ago, and the infrared glow that betrays it

concepts.title: A Colour Cooked in a Furnace
concepts.contentHtml:
Blue pigments are hard to get from nature. Lapis lazuli and turquoise were precious stones, so about 5,000 years ago Egyptian craftsmen did something new: they made a blue. Egyptian blue is a calcium copper silicate, CaCuSi₄O₁₀, and it is the oldest synthetic pigment known, already in use in Egypt around 3000 BCE.1 It was used as a substitute for expensive minerals like turquoise and lapis lazuli and painted on wood, stone and cartonnage, a papier-mâché-like material.

Making it was genuine chemistry. You need sand (silica), a calcium compound such as lime, a copper source and a flux of soda, all held at high heat for hours until they react into new blue crystals. In 2025 a team led by John McCloy of Washington State University, working with the Carnegie Museum of Natural History and the Smithsonian's Museum Conservation Institute, recreated the pigment with 12 different recipes. They heated mixtures of silicon dioxide, copper, calcium and sodium carbonate at about 1,000 °C for between one and 11 hours, then compared the results with two ancient Egyptian objects.

The surprises came under the microscope. Small differences in the process gave very different results, from deep blue to dull grey or green. The researchers found that the bluest colour requires only about 50 per cent of the blue compound itself; the rest of each grain can be other material.2 Every pigment particle was a mixture, far from uniform. That fits what the team suspects about ancient production: some people made the pigment, others carried it, and it was finally used somewhere else.

Why does it look blue? Its colour comes from copper ions absorbing part of the visible spectrum, the kind of electronic transition you may know from crystal field theory. Egyptian blue matters in the history of colour because it is the earliest known pigment that people manufactured rather than found. Every later synthetic colour in this topic, from Prussian blue to YInMn blue, follows its lead. McCloy's samples went on display at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh.

concepts.title: The Infrared Glow That Finds Lost Paint
concepts.contentHtml:
Egyptian blue hides a property no ancient painter could have known about. Shine red or green light on it and it emits infrared radiation, invisible to your eyes but easy for a digital camera to record.1 The conservation scientist Giovanni Verri published a way to exploit this in 2009, now called visible-induced luminescence imaging. Because even the smallest particles glow, a sculpture that looks plain white in daylight can light up in an infrared photograph, showing exactly where blue paint once lay.

The best-known test is the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum, London: marble figures carved in the fifth century BC for the temple of Athena on the Athenian Acropolis. For centuries they were admired for their white brilliance. In a study published in the journal Antiquity in 2023, Verri, of the Art Institute of Chicago, worked with the British Museum and King's College London and found a "wealth of surviving paint". The blue shows water, from which the sun god Helios rises with his chariot. It fills the empty space between the legs of the stools on which the goddesses Demeter and Persephone sit. Most extensively, it forms designs on woollen garments, such as the mantle of a figure believed to be the goddess Dione. Small traces of white and purple turned up too, and the purple was apparently not the costly shellfish kind.

This overturns a powerful myth. For a long time many people believed that ancient Greek art used only white marble, partly because paint wears away outdoors and partly because restorers sometimes removed surviving traces to restore an assumed original whiteness.2 The carving itself points the other way: the sculptors shaped surfaces to evoke wool, linen and skin, as if expecting painters to finish the effect. Verri is careful about the limits, though. The method sees only Egyptian blue, so it is still difficult to say exactly how the sculptures looked when they were first displayed.

concepts.title: Lost, Then Found in a Roman Recipe
concepts.contentHtml:
The Romans loved Egyptian blue, and the architect Vitruvius left the clearest ancient account of how to make it. Blue, he says, was first manufactured at Alexandria and afterwards by a man called Vestorius at Pozzuoli, near Naples. Sand is ground with natron, a natural soda, until it is as fine as flour; coarse filings of Cyprian copper are added and the paste is rolled into balls, dried and fired in an earthen vessel in a furnace. In one English translation: "Thus the copper and sand heating together by the intensity of the fire, impart to each other their different qualities, and thereby acquire their blue colour.1"

Egyptian blue was virtually the only blue pigment used in Greece and Rome. Then the knowledge faded. Analysts have found it in a few medieval and even Renaissance paintings, but by the Renaissance the knowledge of how it was made was largely forgotten.2 When modern chemists set out to reconstruct the ancient process, Vitruvius's short passage was among the best evidence they had. The Egyptians were not alone, either: in imperial China a related compound, Han blue, a barium copper silicate (BaCuSi₂O₆), has a similar composition, properties and colour.

Today the old blue is having a second career. Because it emits near-infrared light that people cannot see, researchers are exploring it for fingerprint detection and counterfeit-proof inks, and its chemistry resembles that of some high-temperature superconductors. A colour first made for tombs and temples has turned into a modern optical material, and the same glow that helps conservators find it on the Parthenon makes it useful in a forensic laboratory.

title: Ultramarine: The Blue Beyond the Sea
description: Lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, a recipe of wax and lye, and what blue cost a painter

concepts.title: From an Afghan Mine to the Virgin's Robe
concepts.contentHtml:
Ultramarine means "beyond the sea". The medieval Latin name, ultramarinus, recalls that the stone it came from was imported from Asia. That stone is lapis lazuli, a mixture of limestone, silicate minerals and pyrite whose blue part is the mineral lazurite. In the Middle Ages it was mined only in Afghanistan, in the mines of Badakhshan, and pigment from there travelled more than 6,000 km to reach Germany.1

Its chemistry is unusual. Lazurite is a complex sodium aluminium silicate containing sulfur, roughly Na₇Al₆Si₆O₂₄S₃, and its intense blue is caused by an unpaired electron in S₃⁻, an ion of three sulfur atoms carrying a negative charge. So the colour comes not from a metal ion, as in Egyptian blue, but from a radical, a species with an odd electron.2 Ultramarine survives high temperatures and alkali, so it can even be used in fresco, but dilute acid destroys it, releasing hydrogen sulfide.

Grinding the stone is not enough. Around 1400 the Italian painter Cennino Cennini warned in his handbook that the blue is mixed with "what is like ashes", and that the finer you grind it, the paler the result. His method: pound and grind the lapis, then knead the powder into a paste with melted pine resin, mastic and new wax, keeping your hands oiled with linseed oil, and leave it for at least three days and nights. Then knead the paste in warm lye, like bread dough. The blue washes out into the lye and sinks; you pour it off and repeat with fresh lye for several days, until the paste no longer tints the lye and is thrown away. The first extracts are the best.

The finest blue went where it mattered most. In Christian Europe, ultramarine became the colour of the Virgin Mary's robes, which is why its absence is so telling in the next story.

concepts.title: Waiting for Blue: Michelangelo and Vermeer
concepts.contentHtml:
In the National Gallery in London hangs The Entombment, an oil painting on wood roughly a metre and a half square, which Michelangelo began after a commission of 1500, probably for a funerary chapel in the church of Sant'Agostino in Rome. Six tall, pale figures surround the body of Christ as he is carried up steps towards a tomb in a dark rocky outcrop, with an olive-green landscape and misty blue hills behind. In the bottom right corner is a gap, a patch of bare underpaint where a kneeling figure should be.

That figure was probably meant to be the Virgin Mary. The gallery's explanation is that Michelangelo would have needed ultramarine made from lapis lazuli for her mantle, and may have been waiting until the last moment to add it, because it was the most expensive pigment and possibly hard to obtain.1 His other unfinished panel there, the Manchester Madonna, is missing its ultramarine too. In 1501 he went back to Florence, probably to claim the marble block that became his David, and the painting was never finished.

How costly was it? In medieval Europe ultramarine was as rare and expensive as gold, and patrons commonly specified in writing how much of it they would buy for the artist to use. In the 17th century the Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer still used it lavishly. When the Mauritshuis in The Hague examined his Girl with a Pearl Earring (about 1665) in 2018, the team traced the ultramarine in her headscarf to lapis lazuli from what is now Afghanistan. "This blue pigment was more valuable than gold in the 17th century," said the project leader, Abbie Vandivere.

The same study found a surprise behind the girl. In her yellow jacket, white collar and blue headscarf, she seems to float in front of a dark, empty space. In fact Vermeer painted her in front of a green curtain, which has faded from view over the centuries.2 Even the white of the famous pearl came from far away: the lead white in it was traced to the Peak District in northern England.

concepts.title: The Woman with Blue Teeth
concepts.contentHtml:
Archaeologists studying dental plaque under the microscope once noticed something odd in the teeth of a middle-aged woman buried at Dalheim in Germany, in the grounds of a ruined monastery that had once housed a community of nuns. She had lived in the 11th century. Trapped in her hardened plaque, the dental calculus, were more than 100 particles of a deep blue.1

A team from the University of York and the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History identified the blue with Raman spectroscopy, which uses the scattering of laser light to reveal a crystal's structure. It was lazurite, the blue component of lapis lazuli: the particles were ultramarine. Their 2019 paper in Science Advances asked how a pigment as costly as gold ended up in a woman's mouth.

The most likely answer is that she was a painter of books. The researchers suggest the pigment entered her mouth as she repeatedly licked her brush to a fine point to paint intricate detail on manuscripts, a technique mentioned in artists' manuals of the time.2 They weighed the alternatives. She might have breathed in dust while preparing the pigment for someone else, or taken lapis as a medicine, since first-century Greek medical texts recommend it for complaints from scorpion bites to ulcers. Both seemed less convincing, given the high cost of ultramarine and the lack of evidence for medicinal use in medieval Germany.

Why does it matter? Early scribes and illuminators rarely signed their work before the 15th century, and historians have widely assumed that monks made most medieval books. Every manuscript produced at Dalheim was destroyed when fire swept the monastery in the 14th century, so these blue specks are the only surviving evidence of a woman's work there. Only the most skilled scribes and painters were trusted with ultramarine, so she was probably one of them.

title: Snails, Insects, Urine and Mummies
description: Colours from living things, and which of the strange stories about them are true

concepts.title: Purple from Snails, Crimson from Insects
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every historic colour came from rocks. Tyrian purple, named after the city of Tyre in today's Lebanon, is the most famous dye of antiquity, and it came from sea snails. Its main component is 6,6′-dibromoindigo: the same molecular skeleton as indigo, the blue of denim, with two bromine atoms attached. The snails make it in minute amounts. When the chemist Paul Friedländer first identified its structure in 1909, he needed 12,000 snails of the species Murex brandaris to produce 1.4 grams of pure dye.1 No wonder it was always very costly.

Notice the word dye. Tyrian purple was used almost exclusively for dyeing textiles, not as a painter's pigment. That is why the purple on the Parthenon sculptures, from the previous lesson, was interesting: true purple was produced from shellfish and was very valuable in the ancient Mediterranean, but the Parthenon purple apparently was not.

Some reds came from insects. Vermeer's red in Girl with a Pearl Earring is cochineal, made from bugs that live on cactus plants in Mexico and South America.2 To use a dye like this in paint, it is turned into a lake: the colour is fixed onto a colourless mineral powder, such as an aluminium compound, to make insoluble grains.

Organic colours like these carry a weakness that most mineral pigments lack: their molecules are fragile. When Van Gogh mixed a cochineal lake into the violet walls of his Bedroom, he chose a colour that has since largely vanished. The last lesson shows what that did to the painting, and how conservators worked out what is missing.

concepts.title: Indian Yellow: The Cows and the Mango Leaves
concepts.contentHtml:
For centuries painters in India, and later in Europe and the United States, used a glowing yellow-orange called Indian yellow. It has been identified on Mughal and Rajput miniature paintings from the 16th to the 19th centuries, and a 2017 study found it used extensively in the wall paintings of the Badal Mahal in Garh Palace at Bundi in Rajasthan, painted in 1620–30 with scenes of courtly life. Its colouring matter is a crystalline mixture of the magnesium and calcium salts of euxanthic acid, and it is noticeably luminescent.

Then there is the story everyone tells. One of the most frequently cited accounts, published by T. N. Mukharji in 1883, says the pigment came from the urine of cows fed solely on mango leaves.1 The diet allegedly killed the cows young, and that supposedly led to a ban on production. Indian yellow was made until the end of the 19th or the beginning of the 20th century. It sounds like a tall tale, and some scholars, including the writer Victoria Finlay, have questioned both the method and the reason the pigment disappeared.

The chemistry, though, fits the story surprisingly well. Mango leaves contain euxanthone, or a precursor of it. Early studies showed that mammals such as cows or rabbits can combine it with glucuronic acid, one of the body's standard ways of tagging a molecule for disposal, and excrete the product as a salt of euxanthic acid.2 Euxanthic acid, in other words, is exactly the kind of molecule a body makes. The 2017 team, led by Charlotte Martin de Fonjaudran, also found a related sulfonated compound, which mammals produce by a parallel route.

So is the legend proven? Not quite. The same authors point out that plants also have the enzymes that make sulfonated compounds, so that finding cannot by itself validate the animal-based method. The fairest verdict is that the cow-urine account is plausible and chemically consistent, but neither confirmed nor debunked.

concepts.title: Mummy Brown: Painting with the Dead
concepts.contentHtml:
From at least the 16th century until the early 1900s, European painters could buy a rich, transparent brown called mummy brown, made from ground-up Egyptian mummies, typically mixed with a drying oil such as walnut.1 It grew out of medicine. From the early medieval period Europeans swallowed and applied preparations of mummy as cures, and early artists' pigments were commonly sold alongside medicines in apothecaries' shops. Recipes varied wildly, some calling for the whole body and others for "only the finest muscle".

Napoleon's invasion of Egypt at the end of the 18th century set off a craze for all things Egyptian, and boatloads of mummies were shipped to Europe as fuel for steam engines, fertiliser and art supplies. The London colourman C. Roberson listed mummy brown in its catalogue until 1933. By then supply was the problem: an 1898 article in Scientific American complained that good mummies were being kept for museums, and in 1964 a member of the Roberson firm told Time magazine that they "might have a few odd limbs lying around somewhere", but not enough to make any more paint.

Not every painter was comfortable. When Lawrence Alma-Tadema told Edward Burne-Jones what the paint was made of, Burne-Jones fetched his tube from the studio and buried it in the garden. His nephew Rudyard Kipling remembered him announcing that he had discovered it was made of dead Pharaohs and they must bury it accordingly.2

Here is the twist. You may read that a particular masterpiece, such as Eugène Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, his painting of the 1830 Paris uprising in the Louvre, contains real mummy. Delacroix did use mummy brown, but it is almost impossible to show that any specific painting contains it.3 Mummy recipes varied, embalming resins such as mastic were also ordinary varnishes, and the molecules that would prove a mammal origin would be present only in tiny amounts, so even mass spectrometry cannot settle it.

title: Beautiful Poisons
description: Lead white, vermilion and the arsenic greens that coloured Victorian homes

concepts.title: Lead White: Made in Dung, Dangerous in the Studio
concepts.contentHtml:
For more than two thousand years the most important white in painting was lead white, basic lead carbonate. It was the main white pigment used by artists until the 19th century, for grounds, for lightening other colours and for painting light itself.1 In the fourth century BC the Greek writer Theophrastus described how to make it: a piece of lead is placed above vinegar in a cask, and after about ten days a kind of mildew is scraped from the lead.

Later makers scaled the recipe up. Strips of lead were set in porous earthenware pots over weak vinegar, in sheds packed with fermenting manure.2 The rotting dung supplied both heat and carbon dioxide, and over a few months the acid and carbon dioxide turned the surface of the lead into a white crust, which was scraped off, dried and ground. In oil the pigment had a bonus: it acts as a catalyst for the drying of the oil.

Every painter who ground it, mixed it or licked a brush was handling a poison. A 2012 history of lead poisoning by Michele Augusto Riva and colleagues argues that among Renaissance workers the painters were probably the most exposed, and names Piero della Francesca, Rembrandt and Francisco Goya as painters who may have been victims.3 That "may" matters. Diagnosing someone dead for centuries is guesswork, so be wary of confident claims that lead explains a particular artist's illness or style. Around 1700 the Italian physician Bernardino Ramazzini identified the lead-processing techniques of potters, tinsmiths and painters as dangerous, and described potters with palsied hands, colic and lost teeth.

The pigment was not easily given up. In 1921 the International Labour Office drew up the White Lead (Painting) Convention to ban the indoor use of lead paint, and Britain never ratified it. Artists finally switched to the less toxic zinc white and titanium white in the 20th century.

concepts.title: Vermilion: The Mercury Red That Turns Black
concepts.contentHtml:
The most brilliant red of the old masters was vermilion, mercury(II) sulfide, HgS. Its oldest form is the ground mineral cinnabar, but it can also be made. Mercury reacted with molten sulfur gives a black form of mercury sulfide, which becomes red when it is sublimed, vaporised and condensed again. A cheaper wet process later converted the black form to red by heating it in a solution of ammonium or potassium sulfide. You met vermilion in the robes of the Buddhas at Bamiyan.

Vermilion has an infamous flaw: it can darken to grey or black. Marika Spring and Rachel Grout of the National Gallery examined ten paintings and found vermilion turned completely grey in some areas and lilac-grey in others. Under the microscope the change was a thin blackened layer over coarser white and black material, with unaltered red beneath. Raman spectroscopy identified the white as calomel, mercury(I) chloride.1 Where did the chlorine come from? The unaltered vermilion was chlorine-free, so they suggested dirt, perhaps sodium chloride from skin debris. Where a glaze covered the red, it had been protected from both dust and light.

The black part has been argued over for years, which makes it a good example of how conservation science works. In 2005 Katrien Keune and Jaap Boon proposed that light converts some vermilion into mercury and sulfur, with chloride ions acting as a catalyst, and that nanoparticles of metallic mercury on the surface turn it black. Metallic mercury is volatile, so it is hard to catch in the act. In 2013 Koen Janssens of the University of Antwerp and colleagues placed the pigment in chlorine-containing water, shone laser light on it until it blackened, and showed that it released ions at exactly the voltage expected for metallic mercury. Salty air and light, in other words, can make liquid metal from red paint.2

concepts.title: Death in the Wallpaper: The Arsenic Greens
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1775 the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered a new green pigment that contained arsenic, copper arsenite.1 Scheele's green became hugely popular in paints, fabrics and wallpapers. In 1814 a company in Schweinfurt, Germany, began making a more vivid relative, emerald green, also called Paris green or Schweinfurt green: copper acetoarsenite, made by combining copper acetate with arsenic trioxide. Victorian England was bathed in it; by 1860 more than 700 tons had been produced there.

Everyone knew arsenic was poisonous, yet the colour was cheap and fashionable. Wallpapers shed toxic green dust onto food and floors, and illness and even death were often blamed on papers described as "highly arsenical". In 1879 the wallpaper makers Jeffrey & Co. invited a chemist from the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich to test their products, and he declared them free of poisonous substances. Yet emerald green was never actually prohibited.2 Its use died out on its own, either because of its toxic reputation or because the colour simply went out of fashion. (Napoleon's rooms on St Helena were papered in Scheele's green; the History's Cold Cases topic explains why that cannot be the whole story of the arsenic in his hair.)

The greens still lurk on library shelves. In 2019 Melissa Tedone, a conservator at the Winterthur Museum, Garden & Library in Delaware, noticed green colour flaking off an 1857 book, Rustic Adornments for Homes of Taste. X-ray fluorescence found copper and arsenic, and Raman spectroscopy confirmed emerald green. The bookcloth carried an average of 1.42 milligrams of arsenic per square centimetre; a lethal dose for an adult is roughly 100 milligrams.3 Her Poison Book Project has since tested about 350 green books at Winterthur and found arsenic in about 10 per cent. The advice is not to panic or throw them away but to handle them with nitrile gloves and store them in sealed plastic bags.

title: Colour from the Laboratory
description: Prussian blue, chrome yellow, French blue and the paint tube that went outdoors

concepts.title: Prussian Blue: The First Modern Synthetic
concepts.contentHtml:
In Berlin in 1706 a colour maker and former army officer, Johann Jacob Diesbach, and the theologian and alchemist Johann Conrad Dippel came upon a new blue.1 Historians call the discovery serendipitous, a lucky accident. Some sources give the date as 1704, but the historian of chemistry Alexander Kraft, drawing on newer research, dates it to 1706. Named after its home, Prussian blue (or Berlin blue) is the oldest modern synthetic pigment, and it is still in use today.2

Chemically, its usual formula is Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃·xH₂O: iron(III) ions combined with hexacyanoferrate ions, in which an iron(II) ion is surrounded by six cyanide groups. Iron in two charge states, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, sits in one solid, and the deep blue arises from that combination. You can make it in a beaker by mixing solutions of iron(III) chloride and potassium ferrocyanide, when a blue solid drops out of solution.

At first its makers kept the recipe secret. It was finally made public when Caspar Neumann, the Royal Court Apothecary in Berlin, passed it to the Royal Society in London for anonymous publication, which came in 1724. From there Prussian blue travelled the world. Dutch traders carried it to Japan, where it was called Berurin-ai, Berlin blue, and it reached Edo (now Tokyo) in 1829.3 Compared with the plant indigo that printmakers had used, it was bold and vivid, with a wide range of tones and more resistance to fading, ideal for water and sky. In 1831 the publisher Nishimuraya Yohachi advertised Katsushika Hokusai's new series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji as prints "in blue", and ten prints from the series, including the Great Wave, were printed in Prussian blue.4 The Great Wave shows a high wave about to break in a rough sea, with three rowing boats braving the waves and Mount Fuji in the background; the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam holds an impression, a colour woodblock print 25.4 by 37.5 cm.

Prussian blue marks a turning point: it was the first of the modern synthetic pigments to come out of a chemist's workshop, and the next century would bring many more.

concepts.title: A Chemist's Shelf: Chrome, Cadmium and French Blue
concepts.contentHtml:
After 1800, new elements and compounds poured out of laboratories, and painters' palettes changed fast. In 1797 the French chemist Louis Vauquelin discovered the element chromium.1 Soon afterwards lead chromate was recognised as a pigment, and chrome yellow was in use by the first quarter of the 19th century. Cadmium yellow, cadmium sulfide, followed from about 1840. A new cobalt blue, made from cobalt and aluminium oxides, arrived in the early 19th century. You met another product of this era, emerald green, in the previous lesson.

The most dramatic story concerns ultramarine. Natural ultramarine still cost a fortune, so in 1824 the Société d'Encouragement pour l'Industrie Nationale in France offered a prize of 6,000 francs for a synthetic ultramarine that could be sold for less than 300 francs a kilo. In February 1828 the prize went to Jean-Baptiste Guimet, even though his process cost 400 francs a kilo, while genuine ultramarine was fetching up to 4,000.2 Christian Gmelin of the University of Tübingen challenged Guimet's claim, and rival factories in France and Germany began making each man's version. The new pigment quickly became known as "French blue" or "permanent blue".

Think about what that did to meaning. In the Middle Ages ultramarine on a painting was itself a display of wealth, written into contracts. Once it could be made in a factory for a tenth of the price, a painter's choice of blue no longer told you much about a patron's purse. In the 20th century Yves Klein, working with the pigment dealer Edouard Adam, suspended ultramarine in a synthetic resin to create his trademark International Klein Blue.

concepts.title: Paint in a Tube: Did It Make Impressionism?
concepts.contentHtml:
Before the 1840s, an oil painter's ready-mixed colours were awkward to carry. They were commonly sealed in a pig's bladder tied with string, which you had to stab with a syringe to get at the paint, or kept in glass tubes that also needed a syringe. Storing paint once it was mixed with oil had been a problem for centuries.

The answer came from an American portrait painter living in England, John Goffe Rand. On 11 September 1841 he patented "metal rolls for paint": collapsible tubes of thin metal, best made of tin, with a screw cap.1 You squeezed out a dab and closed the cap, and the rest stayed fresh. The London colour makers Winsor & Newton were quick to sell paints in Rand's tubes. Rand himself did less well: he lost everything investing in the rights to a modified piano and went home as poor as he had left.

The famous claim is that the tube made Impressionism possible. Pierre-Auguste Renoir is quoted as saying: "Without paints in tubes there would have been no Cézanne, no Monet, no Sisley or Pissarro, nothing of … Impressionism." There is truth in it. A painter with a box of tubes could carry a full palette into a field and work quickly in changing light, using the bright new colours of the age.

But it is only part of the story. Artists had been painting in the open air for several decades before, especially in France, and portable easels and paint boxes may have mattered just as much.2 The fair verdict is that the tube made outdoor painting easier rather than inventing it, and it soon became the standard way to sell artists' paint. The topic Why Is This Art? picks up what the Impressionists did with that freedom.

title: Colours That Change, Colours to Come
description: Fading reds, browning sunflowers, YInMn blue and the fight over the blackest black

concepts.title: Van Gogh's Bedroom Was Not Blue
concepts.contentHtml:
In October 1888, in Arles in the south of France, Vincent van Gogh painted his bedroom in the Yellow House, which he had furnished himself with simple furniture and hung with his own paintings. The bright colours were meant to express absolute "repose". The rear wall seems to meet the side wall at an odd angle, but that is not a mistake: the corner really was skewed. He flattened the space and left out shadows on purpose, so that the picture would resemble a Japanese print. This version, oil on canvas, 72.4 by 91.3 cm, is in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam. He painted two more, now in the Art Institute of Chicago and the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.

Today you see blue walls and doors, but according to the Van Gogh Museum the walls and doors were originally purple rather than blue, and much of the strong contrast you see now is the result of discolouration.1 Analysis published by Johanna Salvant showed that the walls and doors were painted in cobalt blue mixed with carmine, a cochineal red lake.2 Carmine is unstable, and as it broke down the violet turned blue. The floor has drifted towards blue as well, because its red lakes, carmine and geranium lake, have faded.

Van Gogh was fond of fragile reds. Eosin, sold as geranium lake, was reportedly one of his favourite pigments, and it is one of the red lakes most prone to fading.3 A 2021 study of his Landscape with Snow and Mountains at Saint-Rémy, both in the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, detected eosin in areas that are now severely faded. Conservators can work out the lost colours from microscopic samples, spectroscopy and paint reconstructions, but they cannot simply put a vanished red back: that would mean adding new paint to Van Gogh's own.

concepts.title: Why the Sunflowers Are Turning Brown
concepts.contentHtml:
Van Gogh's Sunflowers are among the most famous yellow paintings in the world. In Arles in 1888–89 he painted repetitions of the subject: sunflowers against a yellow background, above a light-yellow table. Three of them hang in the National Gallery in London, in a museum in Tokyo and in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam. Their glow came from chrome yellows, lead chromate pigments ranging from lemon to orange-yellow. For decades experts debated whether the differences in yellow between versions were Van Gogh's choice or damage.1

The chemistry behind the debate is a redox reaction, the kind you may have met in Atoms & Bonding. Chrome yellow contains chromium in its highest oxidation state, Cr(VI). Under light, some kinds of chrome yellow are reduced to Cr(III), which darkens the paint. Earlier experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility had shown that the sulfate-rich, lemon-yellow variety, PbCr₁₋ₓSₓO₄, is far more likely to darken than orange-yellow PbCrO₄, the most lightfast of the family.

In 2015 Letizia Monico, Koen Janssens and colleagues examined the Amsterdam painting itself. Scanning macro X-ray fluorescence and Raman spectroscopy mapped where each kind of yellow lies without touching the picture, and found both the lightfast and the light-sensitive types, often mixed with other pigments such as vermilion, zinc white and emerald green. Two microscopic samples then went to the synchrotron, whose intense X-rays can read chromium's oxidation state. In one region, about 35 per cent of the chromium was Cr(III) in a layer 2–3 micrometres thick, right where the paint meets the varnish, while the yellow paint beneath was unchanged.2

The verdict: the Sunflowers really are changing, at least in places. The team mapped the areas at highest risk so the museum can monitor them and light the painting more safely. It is a lesson for anyone who judges a painter's colours by what hangs on the wall today.

concepts.title: A New Blue and the Blackest Black
concepts.contentHtml:
The story of pigments is not finished. In 2009 Mas Subramanian and his students at Oregon State University were making new materials for electronics, heating mixtures to over 2,000 °F (about 1,100 °C).1 A graduate student, Andrew E. Smith, took one mix out of the furnace and found it a startling blue. YInMn blue, named after its yttrium, indium and manganese oxides, absorbs red and green light and reflects blue. It also reflects heat and is extremely stable. The Shepherd Color Company licensed it in 2016, and in 2017 it inspired a Crayola crayon called Bluetiful.

You may read that YInMn was the first new blue in 200 years. Hyperallergic, which once described it that way, corrected itself: it is the first new inorganic blue pigment in that time, the last having been cobalt blue in the early 19th century.2 Subramanian would add that nobody discovered a colour at all, only a material.

At the other extreme is Vantablack, developed by Surrey NanoSystems in Britain for military and astronomy uses. It is made of microscopic vertical tubes: light that strikes it is trapped between them instead of bouncing back, and it absorbs about 99.96 per cent of the light.3 The company allowed the sculptor Anish Kapoor to be the only artist able to use it, and many artists were furious. In 2016 Stuart Semple released the "world's pinkest pink" at £3.99 a pot for anyone except Kapoor; buyers had to declare they were not Kapoor. Kapoor got some anyway and posted a photo of his middle finger dipped in it.

Then, in 2019, MIT engineers grew a carbon nanotube coating that captures at least 99.995 per cent of incoming light, ten times blacker, and used it to make a $2 million yellow diamond look like a flat black void.4 Who should own a colour, or a material that makes one? The argument is still going.
